title_patterns: [EVENT/ASSET] just [past-tense verb of completed action] — now what?  (closed-loop event + forward question, no prediction in the title)
[NAMED CREDIBLE SOURCE], [their title/firm]: [their specific claim in their own words]  (attribution-first framing that outsources the opinion)
[COMPANY] reports [specific directional result] for [exact quarter/period]  (plain reporting shape, period named explicitly)
EARNINGS/DATA ALERT: [2-3 tickers, comma-separated]  (all-caps label + ticker list, zero adjectives)
[POLICY/INSTITUTIONAL ACTION] on [market behavior] — what actually changes  (mechanism over outrage)
Key takeaways from [first/latest specific report or filing]  (numbered-insight promise anchored to a document)
[YEAR] setup for [index/sector], according to [named analyst/firm]  (year + attribution, avoids self-made forecast)
[SEGMENT/COHORT] is now [specific measured behavior with unrounded figure]  (data observation about a group, no verdict)
hook_patterns: Lead with the single hardest number and its exact source in the first sentence, then say what it is being compared against.
State what was expected vs what was printed, in that order, before any interpretation.
Name the document/filing/transcript you are reading from, then quote the one line that matters.
Open with the timeline: 'Three weeks ago X was priced at A. As of yesterday's close it is B.' Then ask what changed.
Acknowledge the loud narrative in one sentence, then say 'here is what the data supports and what it doesn't.'
packaging_notes: Two clear duration clusters: 45-90s clips built around one number or one quote, and 14-16 min explainers. The 7-8 min single-topic breakdown is the reliable middle lane.
Past-tense completed-event verbs ('just popped', 'reports', 'passes') outperform future-tense speculation — describe what already happened and let the analysis carry the forward view.
Attribution is a legitimacy multiplier: naming a real analyst, firm, or official document in the title lets you carry a strong claim without becoming the hype source.
Specific, unrounded figures and exact periods (quarter, close time, dollar amount) beat vague magnitude words; avoid 'massive', 'huge', 'wild' — they are doing the work that a number should do.
A trailing open question ('now what?') or 'what actually changes' outperforms declarative doom framing, and keeps the promise inside what data can answer.
Recurring format labels (ALERT-style prefixes, 'Key takeaways from') build repeat-view habit at low production cost and signal reporting rather than opinion.
